entries.1:1: Paul opens by saying his authority as a messenger of Jesus did not come from any human being or group. It means his message should be taken as coming from God himself, not from people.
entries.1:2: Paul includes the believers who are with him in sending this letter to the churches scattered across the region of Galatia. It shows this is a shared greeting from a wider group of Christians, not just one man.
entries.1:3: Paul wishes his readers kindness and peace that come from God the Father and Jesus Christ. It is a blessing that reminds them where real peace is found.
entries.1:4: Jesus gave up his own life to deal with our sins and to rescue us from the evil way of the world around us. It means his sacrifice was intentional and was part of God's plan to free us.
entries.1:5: Paul gives all honor and praise to God forever. It is a short burst of worship, reminding readers that God deserves the credit for what Jesus did.
entries.1:6: Paul is shocked that the Galatians are quickly turning away from the God who called them by his grace, toward a different message. It means they were drifting from the true gospel surprisingly fast.
entries.1:7: That other message is not really good news at all; some people are just stirring up trouble and twisting the message about Christ. It means not every religious message is genuine, even if it sounds like good news.
entries.1:8: Paul says that even if he himself or an angel from heaven preached a different message, that preacher should be condemned. It means the true gospel is so important that no one, however impressive, may change it.
entries.1:9: Paul repeats the warning: anyone who preaches a different message than the one they received should be condemned. It means this is not a casual opinion but a serious matter he wants them to take to heart.
entries.1:10: Paul asks whether he is trying to win people's approval or God's, and says if he were still pleasing people he would not be serving Christ. It means serving Jesus sometimes means not being popular with everyone.
entries.1:11: Paul tells them the message he preached did not originate with any human being. It means the gospel is not a human invention but something with a higher source.
entries.1:12: Paul did not receive his message from people or learn it in a school; it came to him through Jesus Christ revealing himself. It means his understanding of the gospel came directly from God.
entries.1:13: Paul reminds them how he used to live in the Jewish religion, violently persecuting the church and trying to destroy it. It means his past was well known, which makes his change all the more striking.
entries.1:14: Paul was more devoted to the Jewish religion than many of his peers, deeply committed to the traditions passed down from his ancestors. It means he was not a casual observer but a serious, zealous follower before he met Christ.
entries.1:15: But God, who had set Paul apart even before he was born, chose in his kindness to act. It means God's plan for Paul's life was not an accident but a deliberate act of grace.
entries.1:16: God chose to reveal his Son in Paul so that Paul would tell the good news about Jesus to non-Jewish people. It means Paul's mission came straight from God, and he did not need to check with people first.
entries.1:17: Paul did not go to Jerusalem to consult the apostles who were there before him; instead he went to Arabia and later returned to Damascus. It means he followed God's leading rather than seeking human approval.
entries.1:18: Three years later Paul finally went to Jerusalem to get to know Peter and stayed with him for fifteen days. It means his contact with the leading apostles was brief and came later, not at the start.
entries.1:19: Of the other apostles, Paul saw only James, the brother of the Lord. It means his visit was limited, which supports his point that his message did not come from them.
entries.1:20: Paul calls God as a witness that what he is writing is true. It means he is making a serious, honest claim and wants them to trust his account.
entries.1:21: After that, Paul went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia. It means he continued his work far from Jerusalem, again showing he was not dependent on the apostles there.
entries.1:22: The churches in Judea had never met Paul personally. It means they knew of him only by reputation, not by face-to-face contact.
entries.1:23: They only heard the report that the man who once persecuted them was now preaching the faith he had tried to destroy. It means his dramatic change was spreading as good news among the believers.
entries.1:24: When they heard this, they praised God because of Paul. It means his transformed life led people to honor God rather than Paul himself.
entries.2:1: Paul is saying that fourteen years passed before he went back to Jerusalem, and he took two companions with him. It shows Paul's work moved at its own pace under God, not on human schedules.
entries.2:2: Paul went because God revealed he should, and he explained the message he preached to non-Jews, both openly and privately to the leaders. He wanted to make sure his work was not wasted or undermined.
entries.2:3: Titus was a Greek and was not forced to be circumcised, even though some expected it. This shows that non-Jewish believers are fully accepted without taking on Jewish rituals.
entries.2:4: Some false believers had slipped in to spy on the freedom Christians have in Jesus, hoping to make them slaves to rules. Paul is warning that freedom in Christ is worth protecting.
entries.2:5: Paul refused to give in to them even briefly, so the truth of the good news would stay intact for the readers. Standing firm on the gospel protects what you believe.
entries.2:6: The respected leaders added nothing to Paul's message, and he notes that God does not favor people by status. What matters is the truth of the message, not how important someone seems.
entries.2:7: The leaders saw that Paul had been entrusted with the good news for non-Jews, just as Peter was for Jews. God gives different assignments to different people, and both are valid.
entries.2:8: The same power of God was at work in Peter's mission to Jews and in Paul's mission to non-Jews. God's work is not limited to one group or one leader.
entries.2:9: James, Peter, and John, the respected leaders, shook hands with Paul and Barnabas in agreement, dividing the work between non-Jews and Jews. This shows unity and mutual recognition in spreading the message.
entries.2:10: The only thing they asked was that Paul remember the poor, which he was already eager to do. Caring for those in need is a core part of following Jesus.
entries.2:11: When Peter came to Antioch, Paul opposed him openly because Peter was clearly doing wrong. Even respected leaders can be wrong and need to be corrected.
entries.2:12: Peter used to eat with non-Jewish believers, but he pulled back when certain men came, afraid of criticism from the circumcision group. Fear of people can make us act against what we know is right.
entries.2:13: The other Jewish believers followed Peter's bad example, and even Barnabas was led astray. One person's hypocrisy can pull others off course, so we should be careful who we follow.
entries.2:14: Paul confronted Peter publicly because his behavior did not match the truth of the good news. If you claim to follow Jesus, your actions should line up with what you believe.
entries.2:15: Paul acknowledges that he and Peter were born Jewish, not outsiders to God's people. He is setting up his point by noting their background.
entries.2:16: No one is made right with God by keeping the law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. We trust in Christ to be accepted by God, not in our own rule-keeping.
entries.2:17: If seeking to be right with God through Christ makes us look like sinners, that does not mean Christ leads people into sin. Paul firmly rejects that idea.
entries.2:18: If Paul rebuilt the very rules he had torn down, he would be proving himself a lawbreaker. Going back to old ways after finding freedom in Christ is self-defeating.
entries.2:19: Through the law itself, Paul died to the law's control so he could live for God. The old way of earning approval is over; now life is about belonging to God.
entries.2:20: You are no longer living for yourself; Christ lives in you. Faith is trusting the one who gave himself.
entries.2:21: Paul refuses to treat God's grace as worthless, because if keeping the law could make us right with God, Christ died for nothing. Grace is the whole point of what Jesus did.
entries.3:1: Paul is shocked that the Galatians, who clearly heard about Jesus dying on the cross, have been led away by false teaching. It means believers should stay grounded in what they were first taught about Christ instead of being swayed by convincing but wrong ideas.
entries.3:2: Paul asks one simple question to make them think: did they receive God's Spirit by keeping rules, or by hearing and trusting the message? It means the Christian life starts by faith, not by earning anything.
entries.3:3: Paul points out how inconsistent it is to begin the Christian life by the Spirit and then try to finish it by human effort. It means you don't start with God's grace and then switch to self-effort to complete what He began.
entries.3:4: Paul asks whether all their suffering and experience was wasted, then softens it with hope that it wasn't. It means their struggles were not pointless, and they should not throw away what they had already gone through.
entries.3:5: Paul asks whether God gives His Spirit and works miracles among them because they keep the law or because they believe what they heard. It means God's activity in their lives is a response to faith, not rule-keeping.
entries.3:6: Abraham believed God, and God counted that faith as righteousness. It means being right with God has always come through trusting Him, not through doing enough good things.
entries.3:7: Those who live by faith are the true descendants of Abraham. It means anyone who trusts God belongs to Abraham's family, regardless of background.
entries.3:8: Scripture foresaw that God would make Gentiles right with Him by faith and announced this good news to Abraham in advance. It means God's plan to bless all nations through faith was there from the beginning.
entries.3:9: Those who live by faith share in the blessing promised to Abraham, who trusted God. It means faith connects you to the same blessing Abraham received.
entries.3:10: Anyone relying on keeping the law is under a curse, because the law demands perfect obedience to every command. It means trying to be right with God by rule-keeping puts you in an impossible position, since no one keeps it all.
entries.3:11: It's clear no one is made right with God by the law, because Scripture says the righteous will live by faith. It means God's approval comes through trust, not through law-keeping.
entries.3:12: The law isn't based on faith; it works on the principle that whoever does these things will live by them. It means law and faith are two different approaches, and the law's approach depends on doing, not believing.
entries.3:13: Christ freed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us when He was hung on a tree. It means Jesus took the punishment we deserved so we could be free.
entries.3:14: Christ's work means the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the Gentiles, and believers receive the promised Spirit through faith. It means God's blessing and His Spirit come to everyone who believes, not just one group.
entries.3:15: Paul uses an everyday example: once a human agreement is ratified, no one can cancel or add to it. It means a settled promise is meant to be honored, which sets up his point about God's promise.
entries.3:16: The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and Paul says this points to one person, Christ. It means God's promise was ultimately fulfilled in Jesus.
entries.3:17: The law came 430 years after God's promise, so it can't cancel that earlier agreement. It means God's promise stands firm and isn't undone by later rules.
entries.3:18: If the inheritance came through the law, it wouldn't be based on God's promise, but God freely gave it to Abraham by promise. It means the blessing is a gift based on God's word, not a wage earned by law-keeping.
entries.3:19: The law was added later because of sin, to last until the promised offspring came, and it was delivered through angels by a mediator. It means the law had a temporary purpose and was given through intermediaries, not directly.
entries.3:20: A mediator implies more than one party, but God is one. It means the law involved a go-between, while God's promise to Abraham was given directly by God Himself.
entries.3:21: The law isn't opposed to God's promises; if a law could give life, then righteousness really would come by law. It means the law isn't the enemy, but it simply lacks the power to make anyone alive or right with God.
entries.3:22: Scripture locked everything under sin so that the promise, received by faith in Jesus Christ, could be given to those who believe. It means the law shows everyone is guilty, so that the gift can come to all who trust Christ.
entries.3:23: Before faith came, we were held in custody under the law, waiting for the faith that was to be revealed. It means the law kept people confined until the time when faith in Christ would arrive.
entries.3:24: The law acted like a guardian to lead us to Christ, so that we could be made right with God by faith. It means the law's job was to bring us to Jesus, not to make us righteous on its own.
entries.3:25: Now that faith has come, we are no longer under that guardian. It means once faith in Christ arrives, the law's supervisory role is finished.
entries.3:26: You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. It means trusting Jesus makes you a full member of God's family.
entries.3:27: All who were baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ. It means baptism marks belonging to Christ, and your identity is now wrapped up in Him.
entries.3:28: There is no Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female, because you are all one in Christ Jesus. It means in Christ, differences that usually divide people no longer determine your standing.
entries.3:29: If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise. It means being Christ's makes you part of Abraham's family and a recipient of God's promised inheritance.
entries.4:1: An heir who is still a child has all the family wealth coming to him, but right now he has no more control over his life than a household servant. Being promised something great doesn't mean you have it yet.
entries.4:2: A child heir is watched over by guardians and managers until the date his father set. Someone else decides things for him until the right time comes.
entries.4:3: In the same way, before we knew God's full plan, we were like children ruled by the basic spiritual forces and rules of the world. We were not free; we were controlled.
entries.4:4: When the exact right time came, God sent his Son, born to a woman and born under the law. God kept his timing and entered human life on our terms.
entries.4:5: He came to buy freedom for those trapped under the law and to give us the full standing of sons in God's family. The point is that we move from slavery to belonging.
entries.4:6: Because you really are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, and that Spirit cries out to God as Father. You can call God Father because his Spirit lives in you.
entries.4:7: So you are no longer a servant but a son, and as a son you inherit what God has promised. Your status and your future are secure in God's family.
entries.4:8: Before you knew God, you were slaves to beings that are not really gods at all. You were devoted to things that had no real power to save you.
entries.4:9: Now that you know God—or better, now that God knows you—how can you turn back to those weak, poor rules and want to be slaves to them again? Going back to old bondage makes no sense after being known by God.
entries.4:10: You are carefully observing special days, months, seasons, and years. You are treating religious calendars as if keeping them makes you right with God.
entries.4:11: I am afraid for you, that all my work among you may have been wasted. Paul worries that his effort to teach them the truth is coming to nothing.
entries.4:12: I beg you, brothers, become like me, because I became like you. You have not wronged me. Paul asks them to share his freedom, reminding them they treated him well before.
entries.4:13: You know that it was because of a bodily illness that I first preached the good news to you. His weakness was the reason he ended up sharing the gospel with them.
entries.4:14: Even though my condition was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me; you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus himself. They received him warmly despite his weakness.
entries.4:15: Where is that sense of blessing you had then? I can testify that, if you could have, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Their former devotion to him seems to have faded.
entries.4:16: So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth? Speaking honestly should not turn friends into enemies.
entries.4:17: Those people are eager for you, but not in a good way; they want to shut you out so you will be eager for them. Their attention is really about controlling you.
entries.4:18: It is good to be eagerly sought after for a good purpose at all times, not only when I am with you. Wanting what is good for someone shouldn't depend on who is watching.
entries.4:19: My dear children, I am again in the pain of childbirth for you until Christ is formed in you. Paul cares for them like a parent longing to see them grow into Christ's likeness.
entries.4:20: I wish I could be with you right now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you. He would rather speak gently in person than at a distance.
entries.4:21: Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not hear what the law says? If you choose the law, you should pay attention to what it actually teaches.
entries.4:22: It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. The story sets up two different kinds of sonship.
entries.4:23: The son of the slave woman was born in the ordinary human way, but the son of the free woman was born through God's promise. One came by human effort, the other by God's word.
entries.4:24: These things are symbolic: the two women represent two covenants. One covenant comes from Mount Sinai and gives birth to slaves—that is Hagar. The story pictures two ways of relating to God.
entries.4:25: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children. The earthly system of law-keeping is pictured as slavery.
entries.4:26: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. There is a free, heavenly reality that belongs to those in Christ.
entries.4:27: It is written: Rejoice, you who are barren and have not given birth; cry out, you who have not labored, for the deserted woman has more children than the one who has a husband. God often brings life and fruit where there seemed to be none.
entries.4:28: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. Your place in God's family comes from his promise, not from human effort.
entries.4:29: Just as the son born in the ordinary way persecuted the son born by the Spirit, so it is now. Expect opposition from those who rely on human effort against those born of the Spirit.
entries.4:30: But what does Scripture say? Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman's son will not share the inheritance with the free woman's son. Law-based slavery and promise-based freedom cannot both be your inheritance.
entries.4:31: So then, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman. You belong to freedom, not to slavery.
entries.5:1: Christ has set us free, so we should stay free and not let anyone make us slaves to rules again. For you, that means guarding the freedom Jesus gave you instead of going back to earning God's approval.
entries.5:2: Paul warns that if they rely on circumcision to be right with God, Christ will do them no good. For you, it means adding your own religious efforts to Jesus cancels out what he did for you.
entries.5:3: Anyone who chooses circumcision to be right with God must then keep the whole law perfectly. For you, it means you cannot pick and choose parts of the law; it is all or nothing.
entries.5:4: Those trying to be right with God by keeping the law have cut themselves off from Christ and fallen away from grace. For you, it means trusting your own goodness instead of Jesus leaves you without him.
entries.5:5: We, by the Spirit and through faith, wait for the hope of being made right with God. For you, it means your right standing with God comes through faith and the Spirit, not your own effort.
entries.5:6: In Christ, whether you are circumcised or not does not matter; what matters is faith that shows itself in love. For you, it means God cares about a faith that produces love, not outward religious marks.
entries.5:7: You were running well, so who stopped you from obeying the truth? For you, it means be careful about who you listen to, because bad teaching can pull you off course.
entries.5:8: This persuasion to follow false teaching did not come from God, who called you. For you, it means if a teaching pulls you away from grace, it is not from God.
entries.5:9: A little yeast works through the whole batch of dough. For you, it means a small amount of false teaching can spread and affect your whole faith.
entries.5:10: Paul is confident the Galatians will agree with him, and the one troubling them will face judgment. For you, it means trust that God will deal with those who distort the gospel.
entries.5:11: If Paul were still preaching circumcision, he would not be persecuted, and the offense of the cross would be gone. For you, it means the cross is offensive because it says you cannot save yourself.
entries.5:12: Paul wishes those troubling the church would go all the way and cut themselves off. For you, it means take seriously how destructive false teachers can be to a church.
entries.5:13: You were called to be free, but do not use freedom as an excuse for selfish desires; instead serve one another in love. For you, it means your freedom in Christ should show up as loving service, not self-indulgence.
entries.5:14: The whole law is summed up in one command: love your neighbor as yourself. For you, it means loving others is the practical summary of what God wants from you.
entries.5:15: If you keep biting and devouring each other, watch out that you do not destroy one another. For you, it means fighting within your church or relationships can tear everyone apart.
entries.5:16: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For you, it means letting the Spirit guide your daily choices keeps sinful desires from controlling you.
entries.5:17: The flesh and the Spirit are opposed to each other, so you cannot do whatever you want. For you, it means expect an inner struggle, and let the Spirit win.
entries.5:18: If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. For you, it means the Spirit's guidance, not rule-keeping, is how you live as God's child.
entries.5:19: The works of the flesh are obvious, including sexual immorality, impurity, and sensuality. For you, it means recognize these behaviors as signs of following your sinful nature, not God.
entries.5:20: These include idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, anger, rivalry, divisions, and false teachings. For you, it means God takes seriously both obvious sins and relational sins like anger and division.
entries.5:21: Envy, drunkenness, and similar things keep people out of God's kingdom. For you, it means these behaviors are not minor; they show a life not ruled by God.
entries.5:22: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, and faithfulness. For you, it means these qualities grow in you as you let the Spirit work.
entries.5:23: Gentleness and self-control are also fruit of the Spirit, and no law is against such things. For you, it means these qualities are always right and should mark your life.
entries.5:24: Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. For you, it means you have said no to your sinful nature and should keep saying no to it.
entries.5:25: Since we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in step with the Spirit. For you, it means if the Spirit gave you life, let him direct your everyday steps.
entries.5:26: Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another. For you, it means pride and jealousy damage relationships, so guard against them.
entries.6:1: If someone is caught doing wrong, those who follow the Spirit should gently help them back on track, remembering they could fall too. It means correcting others with kindness, not pride, because you are not immune to temptation.
entries.6:2: Share each other's burdens and struggles, and by doing so you fulfill what Christ taught. It means practical care for others is how you live out your faith.
entries.6:3: If you think you are important when you are really nothing, you are fooling yourself. It means honest self-assessment keeps you from pride.
entries.6:4: Examine your own actions rather than comparing yourself to others, and take satisfaction in your own work. It means focus on your own faithfulness, not on measuring yourself against your neighbor.
entries.6:5: Each person must carry their own load and answer for their own responsibilities. It means you are accountable for your own part, so take it seriously.
entries.6:6: Anyone who receives teaching should share good things with the one who teaches them. It means supporting those who teach you God's word is a fitting response.
entries.6:7: Don't be deceived: God cannot be mocked, because a person reaps what they sow. It means your choices have real consequences, so choose carefully.
entries.6:8: Sowing to your sinful nature leads to death, but sowing to the Spirit leads to eternal life. It means invest your life in what the Spirit wants, because that is what lasts.
entries.6:9: Don't grow tired of doing good, because in due time you will reap a harvest if you don't give up. It means keep doing right even when it feels unrewarded, because the payoff comes later.
entries.6:10: Whenever you have the opportunity, do good to everyone, especially to fellow believers. It means look for chances to help others, prioritizing your spiritual family.
entries.6:11: Paul points out that he wrote this in large letters with his own hand. It means he is emphasizing this message personally and wants them to take notice.
entries.6:12: Those who want to look good outwardly are pushing circumcision only to avoid being persecuted for the cross. It means some people promote rules to protect their reputation rather than to honor Christ.
entries.6:13: Even those pushing circumcision don't keep the law themselves; they just want to boast about your outward conformity. It means don't let others use you to boost their own pride.
entries.6:14: Paul refuses to boast in anything except the cross of Christ, through which the world's values are dead to him and he to them. It means the cross alone is worth your confidence, not outward achievements.
entries.6:15: Whether or not someone is circumcised doesn't matter; what matters is being a new creation. It means outward religious markers mean nothing compared to a transformed life.
entries.6:16: Peace and mercy rest on everyone who lives by this principle, on God's true people. It means blessing comes to those who trust in the new creation rather than outward rules.
entries.6:17: Paul asks that no one trouble him further, since his body bears the scars of serving Jesus. It means his suffering for Christ proves his authority, so stop questioning him.
entries.6:18: Paul closes by asking that the grace of Jesus Christ be with their spirit. It means he ends with a heartfelt wish that they experience God's unearned kindness.
